clue.text: Sounds like tea produced by a lace-worker

indicators.note: the clue says the wanted word is pronounced like a kind of tea, so we go by ear

parts.note: pekoe is a high-grade black tea, said 'pee-koh'

explanation.surface: Someone making lace brews a pot of tea as the work goes on.
explanation.walkthrough: The tea is PEKOE; the lace term sounds the same but is spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A picot is a small decorative loop worked into the edge of lace or embroidery.

clue.text: A workman might do so when going away for punishment

definitions.text: A workman might do so when going away

explanation.surface: A builder packs his tools to leave, and is penalised.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, a workman leaving might 'pack (his) drill'; as one term it is a military punishment of marching in full kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Pack drill is a soldiers' penalty of drilling while carrying a full pack.

clue.text: Conservative woman's bloomer

parts.note: Anna is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A Tory woman makes a gaffe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' looks like a blunder; it is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A canna is a tropical plant grown for its showy flowers, so something that blooms.

clue.text: About the beginning of the year, arrange rises for hard workers

indicators.note: about means around, so the turned word goes round the month
in a down clue rises means the word reads upwards, turned back to front

parts.note: to sort is to arrange
January, abbreviated Jan, opens the year

explanation.surface: Around New Year, people organise promotions for diligent staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rises' turns the word for arrange upwards, giving TROS, which goes round the month. To work like a Trojan is an English idiom for labouring hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To work like a Trojan is to labour tirelessly, from the heroic defenders of Troy.

clue.text: Pub manager shot outside tower

indicators.note: the word for the shot sits around the word for the tower, wrapping it on both sides

parts.note: an inner is a shot hitting the ring just outside the bull on a target
a keep is the main tower of a castle

explanation.surface: A publican has been shot outside a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like a verb about violence; it is a noun, a shot landing in the ring next to the bullseye on a target, and 'outside' wraps it round the tower.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who runs an inn is its landlord, the person who manages a public house.

clue.text: National Assistance set-up in fashionable quarter

indicators.note: the turned word for help goes inside the pair of pieces after it

parts.note: in means fashionable
N, north, is a quarter of the compass

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means written upwards, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: aid is assistance

explanation.surface: The welfare system is established in a trendy district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National Assistance' was a British welfare benefit, but the words part; 'set-up' turns the word for help upwards to give DIA, and 'in' puts it inside the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indian is a citizen of India, one national of that country.

clue.text: Gas briefly identified in the Norwegian capital

definitions.text: Gas briefly identified in the Norwegian capital

parts.words: Gas briefly identified in the Norwegian capital
parts.note: the chemical symbol, a gas's short name, is the capital letter of Norwegian rather than a place in Oslo

explanation.walkthrough: 'Norwegian capital' suggests Oslo, but it means the first letter of 'Norwegian', N, the chemical symbol of this gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrogen is the gas with the element symbol N, the bulk of the air.

clue.text: I include many a pub in the ban

indicators.note: the word for I takes the other pieces into its middle

parts.note: the ego is the self, the I
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: Someone admits putting lots of pubs on the barred list.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held lost its opening 'I', which the printed page shows; 'include' has the word for the self take in the other pieces after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official prohibition, especially on trade.

clue.text: Friend introducing two boys to a style of architecture

parts.note: a pal is a friend
a lad is a boy
Ian is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A friend presents a couple of lads to a building style.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrea Palladio's classical style, much copied in English country houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Palladian architecture follows Palladio's symmetrical classical temple forms.

clue.text: Sail worthy of a king

explanation.surface: A sail fit for a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: A royal is a small sail set above the topgallant on a square-rigged ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The topmost square sail on old rigs carries this name, and the adjective means kingly.

clue.text: Agreement to incorporate new ribbed fabric in outdoor garment

indicators.note: the new fabric goes inside the word for the garment, splitting it in the middle

parts.note: a coat is worn outdoors
cord, short for corduroy, is a ribbed cloth

explanation.surface: A deal is struck to add a new corduroy lining to an overcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to incorporate' is linking padding; 'in' sets the new ribbed cloth inside the garment after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A concordat is a formal treaty, especially one between the Vatican and a state.

clue.text: The Kid's cooking-pot?

explanation.surface: An outlaw of the Wild West is pictured with his camp kettle.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy the Kid was a notorious American outlaw; a billy, or billycan, is a tin pot for cooking over a campfire.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses give the same name: the Western gunman's first name and the Australian bush term for a tin cooking can.

clue.text: Island area a dodo ravaged, finishing up like this

indicators.note: ravaged means torn apart and wrecked, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dodo has wrecked an island region and ended up extinct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ravaged' scrambles ISLAND AREA A DODO into the phrase; the definition 'finishing up like this' fits the extinct dodo too.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something utterly lifeless, as the extinct bird famously is.

clue.text: It's deepest for a short time during the current month

indicators.note: during says the short time falls within the month, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: inst., short for instant, means of the current month in old business letters
a mo, short for moment, is a brief time

explanation.surface: Something is at its lowest point briefly in the course of this month.
explanation.walkthrough: INST is a dated commercial abbreviation for 'this month' (as in 'your letter of the 5th inst.'); MO goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Inmost means furthest in, the innermost or most profound part.

clue.text: Pal involved in ship's officer's plot

indicators.note: involved in means enclosed within, so the word for pal sits inside the officer

parts.note: a mate is an officer on a merchant ship
china is rhyming slang for mate, from china plate

explanation.surface: A friend is mixed up in a scheme by a ship's officer.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' stands for mate, so a pal is a china; 'involved in' sets it inside the ship's officer.
explanation.definitionFit: To machinate is to scheme or contrive intrigues.

clue.text: Completely destroy his model when in a frenzy

indicators.note: a frenzy is wild agitation, so the letters of the two words beside it are thrown about

explanation.surface: A man in a rage smashes the model he has made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when in a frenzy' rearranges HIS MODEL into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To raze a building or argument is to pull it down entirely, leaving nothing.

clue.text: Rowdy behaviour in Arab drama?

explanation.surface: There is rough conduct in an Arabian theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: An Arab is a breed of horse, so a play staged for such horses would be a 'horse play'.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseplay is boisterous rough-and-tumble fun, and split it is a drama for steeds.

clue.text: Cut up board fit only for the scrap-heap

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read upwards, back to front

parts.note: to saw is to cut
a board is a table, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A plank sawn into pieces is only good for the dump.
explanation.walkthrough: SAW read upwards becomes WAS, then TABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wastable can be thrown away as rubbish without loss.

clue.text: Cricketer making the drink available?

explanation.surface: A batsman is the one who gets the drinks served.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket team's first two batsmen are its openers; a bottle opener is what lets you get at a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit one word: the batsman who starts an innings and the gadget that uncaps a bottle.

clue.text: Planner's fiddle takes in novice

indicators.note: takes in means the word for fiddle holds the novice inside it

parts.note: to potter is to fiddle about aimlessly
L, for learner, marks a novice

explanation.surface: An organiser's violin includes a beginner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fiddle' looks like the instrument; it is the verb POTTER, which takes in L for learner.
explanation.definitionFit: A plotter is a schemer who devises secret plans.

clue.text: Old gold coin sewn onto dress

explanation.surface: An ancient coin is stitched on a frock.
explanation.walkthrough: The sequin was an old Venetian gold coin, the zecchino.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one word: the former Italian ducat and the small shiny disc stitched onto clothes.

clue.text: Verbal blunder makes us almost discard the language

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the phrase, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: to slip off a garment is to shed or discard it
a tongue is a language

explanation.surface: A careless remark leads us to give up a language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' clips the last letter of the phrase for discard, giving SLIP OF; 'makes us' is linking padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a lapse is an inadvertent spoken mistake, saying something you did not intend.

clue.text: Plaque produced by council leader in a Manchester suburb

indicators.note: the leader's letter goes inside the place name

parts.note: Sale is a town in Greater Manchester

indicators.note: a leader is the first, so take the opening letter of council

explanation.surface: A commemorative plaque is unveiled by a local council head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plaque' suggests a commemorative tablet; it is the deposit on teeth. C goes inside SALE, a Greater Manchester town.
explanation.definitionFit: Dental scale is the hard deposit that builds up on teeth, also called tartar.

clue.text: Blunder involving a bunch of keys

parts.note: G is a musical key
A is a musical key
F is a musical key
F again as a key
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: Someone makes a mistake with a jangling key ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keys' are musical keys, each a letter from A to G; five of them spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is an embarrassing social mistake.

clue.text: He made violins in the morning, very early!

parts.note: a.m. stands for ante meridiem, in the morning
at one, written AT I with the Roman numeral, is a very early hour of the morning

explanation.surface: A craftsman worked on his instruments before dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: AM plus AT I (at one o'clock, I being the Roman one) gives the name of the famous Cremona family of violin makers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicolò Amati and his family were celebrated Italian luthiers of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

clue.text: An ample lady, Mrs Sullen's mother-in-law

explanation.surface: A plump woman is introduced as Mrs Sullen's husband's mother.
explanation.walkthrough: In Farquhar's comedy The Beaux' Stratagem, Lady Bountiful is the mother of Squire Sullen, so mother-in-law to Mrs Sullen.
explanation.definitionFit: Bountiful means plentiful or generous, and Lady Bountiful is the charitable character in the Farquhar play.

clue.text: Plant even found sheltering right in the grass border

indicators.note: sheltering means the word for even holds the rest inside it

parts.note: e'en is the poetic contraction of even

indicators.note: right goes inside the word for the grass border

parts.note: a verge is the grass strip along the edge of a road

explanation.surface: Even right in the grass along the roadside, a plant is found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' looks like an adverb but is E'EN; R goes into VERGE to make VERGRE, which E'EN shelters.
explanation.definitionFit: An evergreen is a shrub or tree that keeps its leaves all year.

clue.text: Thin maiden abandons medical cure

indicators.note: the maiden leaves the word for the cure, so its letter is removed

parts.note: a remedy is a cure or treatment
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A slim young woman walks away from a treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a maiden is an over with no runs, written M; taking it out of REMEDY leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Reedy describes a voice or figure that is high and thin, like a reed.
